assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED opened a new regime in which a single artificial atom is strongly and controllably coupled to a single microwave photon on a chip. It made dispersive readout, strong coupling, photon-mediated qubit-qubit interaction and later gate-based processors possible. It is the platform through which the macroscopic quantum phenomena recognised in 2025 became a general toolbox. It is a clean physics discovery, not just an application, and I weigh it heavily from my own field.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the Wallraff et al. Nature 2004 strong-coupling experiment are the decisive pair. Schoelkopf led the experimental programme at Yale and Wallraff did the first strong-coupling demonstration. Blais is the lead theory author, while Girvin is an equally defensible fourth name whom the three-laureate cap excludes. I choose Blais, Schoelkopf and Wallraff, but the theory slot is genuinely contestable. I also note that I work close to this community and should be careful about bias.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended in dozens of laboratories over two decades, and the interpretation is stable. It underlies superconducting quantum computing, quantum-limited amplification and microwave quantum optics. Timing is good, especially after the 2025 prize for circuit-level macroscopic quantum effects, though some may argue it is too close in lineage to that prize.
uncertainties: Whether the theory slot should go to Blais or Girvin (or both with Yale colleagues) is unresolved.
Possible perception of overlap with the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize.
My own proximity to this community is a potential bias, not a resolved conflict.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions, and its experimental realisation, established the template for controllable many-body quantum information processing. Ion-trap computers remain the benchmark for gate fidelity and coherence, and the work showed that quantum computation is a physical reality. The foundations also feed quantum simulation.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the clear theoretical originators (1995). Blatt is the leading experimentalist implementing the gates and entanglement of many ions, though Wineland and Monroe also contributed and Wineland already holds a prize. The three-person configuration is plausible but the experimental credit is shared with others not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of replication across laboratories and a clearly demonstrated path to small-scale quantum processors. Some worry that recognition could overlap with the 2012 Wineland-Haroche prize, but the computational and simulation concepts are distinct.
uncertainties: Experimental credit among Blatt, Monroe, Wineland and others is partly outside this candidate's names.
Overlap with the earlier 2012 prize for manipulating individual quantum systems.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical objects into the quantum regime: ground-state cooling, quantum-coherent coupling to light, and phonon states coupled to superconducting qubits. It is a clear case of a new regime of physics opened by careful control of every physical detail, and it links to my own work on phonons coupled to artificial atoms.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer developed radiation-pressure cooling and strong coupling in optical and microwave cavities. Cleland made the first quantum ground state and single-phonon demonstration with a superconducting qubit (O'Connell 2010). Other key people (Painter, Lehnert, Teufel, Schwab) are excluded, so the configuration leaves out real contributors.
assessment.maturity: Several independent groups have confirmed the central results and the field is well established. Applications such as quantum transduction and precision sensing are still developing, but the discovery content, quantum control of macroscopic motion, is solid.
uncertainties: Several equally important contributors (Painter, Lehnert, Teufel) are not among the credited names.
The field is broad and a single discovery statement is hard to define.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model and the superfluid to Mott insulator transition in a controllable setting, with single-site resolution. This turned abstract many-body models into laboratory systems, and the importance for condensed-matter physics is large and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition in 2002, Esslinger realised fermionic Hubbard physics, and Zoller (with Jaksch) supplied the theoretical proposal. Choosing three of four requires dropping either Zoller or one experimentalist. I take the three experimentalists, but the theory credit for the Jaksch-Zoller proposal is a real consideration.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with robust reproducibility across many groups and expanding precision control. Recognition is timely, and some may think it falls too close to the BEC prize of 2001, though the physics is distinct.
uncertainties: The theory credit (Zoller, Jaksch) versus experimental credit allocation is unresolved.
Whether the quantum-simulation benefits have fully delivered beyond proof-of-principle.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, with Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's implementation at record accuracy, opened a new regime of frequency metrology in the 10^-18 range. They enabled tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. The physics is clean and the experimental precision is unquestioned.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and demonstrated the first clocks, and Ye pushed the accuracy and stability to record levels. The two-person configuration is natural, with little attribution dispute, although Hall and Hänsch were recognised for combs in 2005.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups, including NIST, JILA, RIKEN, PTB and others, confirm the performance. The redefinition of the SI second has not yet occurred, but the physical discovery is mature and widely validated.
uncertainties: Overlap in recognition with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and with Dehmelt-Paul-Ramsey-era clock lineage.
Whether the discovery is judged as a technical advance more than a new physical effect.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light brought quantum noise reduction from a theoretical idea to a tool in precision measurement, now used in gravitational-wave detectors to beat the standard quantum limit. It combines a fundamental quantum optics discovery with a verified, concrete benefit in a flagship instrument.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theoretical proposal for squeezed-light interferometry, Kimble produced the first squeezed states and early demonstrations, and Schnabel developed the application in GEO600 and later detectors. Mavalvala, Slusher and Walls are also strong names, so attribution is crowded and partly contested. I pick the three I regard as most decisive for the origin, demonstration and application.
assessment.maturity: Highly confirmed, including operation in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600. The recognition would be timely, although it is complicated by the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across many contributors (Slusher, Walls, Mavalvala, Yuen, Caves) and the three-name cap forces hard choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect introduced a robust new class of quantum matter, with theoretical prediction followed by experimental discovery in HgTe. The ideas of topological protection have spread widely across condensed matter and into quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele predicted the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene; the HgTe prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and its observation by Molenkamp's group are decisive for confirmation. Zhang's death and the exclusion of Bernevig and Hughes complicate fairness. This is outside my main expertise, so I defer to condensed-matter colleagues.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and bulk 3D materials with ARPES. The field is mature and the prize recognition is arguably overdue, although it follows the 2016 topological-phases prize.
uncertainties: Credit for the HgTe prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) is not on the list.
Overlap with the 2016 topological phases prize.
Outside my core expertise; I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on relative merit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg-coupled neutral-atom arrays brought individually controlled atoms with strong tunable interactions into the laboratory, enabling analogue and digital quantum simulation and high-fidelity gates. The platform has rapidly become a competitive route to scalable quantum processors.
assessment.attribution: Saffman's early Rydberg blockade gate proposals, Browaeys's and Lukin's experimental demonstrations of arrays and many-body dynamics all matter. Others (Weiss, Bernien, Greiner, Endres, Jaksch) are also major contributors, so the three names are an incomplete picture.
assessment.maturity: Rapid progress but some results are only a few years old, with independent confirmation across many groups growing. Recognition now would be somewhat premature compared with the other candidates I rank higher, since the practical scalability remains to be demonstrated.
uncertainties: Maturity: much of the evidence is recent, and the key advances in error-corrected logic remain to be consolidated.
Credit is spread across many groups not listed here.
